question_text: Which international agreement, adopted in 2015, aims to limit global warming?
options: The Kyoto Protocol
The Paris Agreement
The Montreal Protocol
The Copenhagen Accord

question_text: What does the 1.5°C target in climate policy refer to?
options: A limit on warming above pre-industrial levels
The maximum average summer temperature in Europe
A cap on annual carbon emissions per person
The temperature at which polar ice will vanish

question_text: Which greenhouse gas is the main driver of recent warming from burning fossil fuels?
options: Water vapour in the atmosphere
Ozone
Methane
Carbon dioxide

question_text: What is the main cause of ocean acidification?
options: Oil spills spreading across the ocean surface
Rising levels of dissolved oxygen in water
Carbon dioxide dissolving into seawater
Plastic waste breaking down into microplastics

question_text: Which body publishes the major scientific assessment reports on climate change?
options: The International Energy Agency
The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change
The World Meteorological Organization
The United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change

question_text: What does the term 'net zero' mean in climate policy?
options: Balancing emissions released and removed
Eliminating every greenhouse gas emission
Reducing emissions to zero immediately
Offsetting emissions only by planting trees

question_text: Which 1987 agreement phased out chemicals that damage the ozone layer?
options: The Basel Convention
The Convention on Biological Diversity
The Kyoto Protocol
The Montreal Protocol

question_text: By what year are the UN Sustainable Development Goals intended to be achieved?
Under the 1951 Refugee Convention, who qualifies as a refugee?
options: Anyone who lacks a valid passport or visa
A person outside their country who fears persecution
A person displaced inside their own country by disaster
Anyone who moves abroad to find better-paid work

question_text: Which UN agency is mandated to protect refugees?
options: The UN Refugee Agency
The World Food Programme
The International Organization for Migration
The UN Children's Fund

question_text: What are 'remittances' in the context of migration?
options: Fees charged by recruitment agencies abroad
Taxes paid by migrants when crossing borders
Payments made by governments to resettle refugees
Money migrants send back to their home country

question_text: What does 'brain drain' describe?
options: The loss of jobs caused by automation
A decline in a country's birth rate
The emigration of highly skilled workers
A shortage of workers caused by an ageing population

question_text: What is a tariff?
options: A ban on trade with another country
A tax on imported goods
A limit on the number of imports allowed
A subsidy paid to domestic farmers

question_text: Which economic theory explains gains from specialising at lower opportunity cost?
options: Comparative advantage
Market equilibrium
Absolute advantage
The Heckscher-Ohlin model

question_text: Which three dimensions does the Human Development Index measure?
options: Exports, imports and currency reserves
Trade, aid and investment flows
Population, land area and resources
Health, education and income

question_text: What is 'inflation'?
options: A fall in the total level of employment
A tax added to imported products
A sustained rise in the general level of prices
A rise in the international value of a currency

question_text: What does the 'digital divide' refer to?
options: The gap between hardware and software costs
Unequal access to digital technology and the internet
Differences in typing speed between office workers
Competition between large technology companies

question_text: What is 'net neutrality'?
options: The principle that all internet traffic is treated equally
A rule requiring websites to register with the government
A ban on paid advertising on social media
A system that blocks harmful websites

question_text: Which description best fits 'disinformation'?
options: Advertising presented as a news article
False content shared by people without intent to deceive
Satire that imitates the style of real news
Deliberately false content spread to mislead people

question_text: What is a 'filter bubble'?
options: A rule limiting how platforms collect personal data
A group of users who report false posts
Isolation caused by personalised content recommendations
A software tool that blocks offensive or harmful websites

question_text: What is 'lateral reading' when checking a claim?
options: Reading an article from start to finish without leaving it
Leaving the page to see what other sources say
Scanning a page for its most common keywords
Comparing two paragraphs within one article

question_text: Which practice best helps verify an image shared online?
options: Running a reverse image search
Counting the number of likes it received
Checking whether the caption is emotional
Sharing it with friends to ask if it is real

question_text: What is 'clickbait'?
options: A link that leads to a broken website
A paid advertisement designed to look like a news article
A correction issued after a factual error
A sensational headline designed to attract clicks

question_text: Why is a random sample important in opinion polling?
options: It makes a survey cheaper to conduct
It removes the need for a margin of error
It helps the sample represent the wider population
It guarantees that the poll will reflect public opinion exactly

question_text: What does 'confirmation bias' mean?
options: Preferring news written in one's first language
Favouring information that supports existing beliefs
Trusting official sources more than stories on social media
Changing one's view after seeing new evidence
